claim: Chain-of-thought prompting with 8 worked exemplars gave state-of-the-art GSM8K accuracy on a 540B model, tested on 3 large models
authors: Wei, Wang, Schuurmans, Bosma, Ichter, Xia, Chi, Le, Zhou
title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
transfer: Baseline step: written reasoning before answer, only for multi-step tasks. Fetch tool gave paraphrase, not verbatim, so quote left empty. The 'gain only at ~100B' claim in the old brief was NOT confirmed here.

claim: Zero-shot 'Let's think step by step' raised text-davinci-002 accuracy from 17.7% to 78.7% on MultiArith and from 10.4% to 40.7% on GSM8K
authors: Kojima, Gu, Reid, Matsuo, Iwasawa
title: Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners
transfer: Cheap trigger phrase as default for arithmetic. Old models; modern models already reason by default (see 12-a-17).

claim: Self-consistency (sample many CoT paths, majority vote) gained +17.9% GSM8K, +11.0% SVAMP, +12.2% AQuA, +6.4% StrategyQA, +3.9% ARC-challenge over greedy CoT
authors: Wang, Wei, Schuurmans, Le, Chi, Narang, Chowdhery, Zhou
title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
transfer: Vote only when the answer is closed and short. Gains shrink as base accuracy rises and for commonsense tasks (+3.9 to +6.4). Verifies the old brief's 'several to 17 points'.

claim: Adaptive-Consistency cuts self-consistency sample budget by up to 7.9x with average accuracy loss under 0.1 point, over 17 datasets and 3 LLMs
authors: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam
title: Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
transfer: Sample one at a time, stop when a lightweight agreement rule fires. Directly supports the probe-then-stop step. Verifies the old brief.

claim: A meta-analysis of over 100 CoT papers plus own tests on 20 datasets and 14 models finds CoT helps mainly on math and logic; on MMLU CoT equals direct answering unless the question or answer contains an equals sign
authors: Sprague, Yin, Rodriguez, Jiang, Wadhwa, Singhal, Zhao, Ye, Mahowald, Durrett
title: To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
transfer: Format gate: CoT on for math/symbolic, direct for recall and multiple choice. Also says a symbolic solver beats CoT: run code instead of reasoning in text. Verifies old brief F1.

claim: CoT lowered accuracy on tasks where deliberation hurts humans (implicit learning, face recognition, classification with exceptions); largest gap 36.3 points absolute (o1-preview vs GPT-4o); on three of six tasks effects were mixed or positive
authors: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths
title: Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
transfer: Do not force reasoning on perception-like or exception-heavy judgments. Note: 36.3 is the gap between the two models, as the abstract words it; the old brief says 'lost up to 36.3 points against GPT-4o', close but check the table.

claim: Explicit CoT prompting now gives small average gains for non-reasoning models, can add variability and break answers the model had right, and gives marginal or no gains on reasoning models while costing far more tokens and time
quote: far more tokens (increasing cost and time) than direct answers
authors: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro
title: Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
transfer: New and missed by old brief. For a modern model, skip the 'think step by step' prompt; rely on native reasoning, and spend tokens only via a check.

claim: Tree of Thoughts raised Game of 24 success from 4% (GPT-4 with CoT) to 74%; also tested on Creative Writing and Mini Crosswords
authors: Yao, Yu, Zhao, Shafran, Griffiths, Cao, Narasimhan
title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
transfer: Search over partial states only where a partial state can be scored cheaply. Single-lab, a task built for search. Verifies old brief F8.

claim: Intrinsic self-correction (no outside feedback) on reasoning tasks struggles and sometimes lowers performance
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
authors: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou
title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
transfer: Revision step must be OFF without a real check. Quote is from the fetch tool, which marked it as the paper's key finding; not seen on the abstract page text itself. Verifies old brief F9.

claim: Critical survey: prompted LLMs have not been shown to self-correct except on tasks unusually suited to it; self-correction works with reliable external feedback; large-scale fine-tuning enables it; many prior studies overstate gains via vague questions or unfair evaluation
authors: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang
title: When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
transfer: Revision rule: revise only from runnable-check output. Use their checklist for our own revision experiments (fair budget, no oracle labels). Verifies old brief.

claim: Models are poor at finding reasoning errors but, given the correct error location, they correct well across five reasoning tasks; a small classifier trained on out-of-domain data finds errors better than prompting a large model
authors: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak
title: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
transfer: New, missed by old brief. Self-correction fails at locating the error, not at fixing it. So localize the error with a program (failing test, unit check, step re-execution), then ask for the fix at that spot.

claim: GPT-4 self-critique caused a significant performance collapse on Game of 24, graph coloring and STRIPS planning; a sound external verifier improved results, and simple re-prompting with it kept most of the benefit
authors: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati
title: On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
transfer: New. Verification by model judgment is unsafe; keep a sound checker in the loop. Simple re-prompt with checker output may be enough, no elaborate machinery.

claim: Reflexion (verbal self-reflection stored in episodic memory, driven by task feedback) reached 91% pass@1 on HumanEval versus GPT-4 at 80%
quote: 91% pass@1 accuracy on the HumanEval coding benchmark
authors: Shinn, Cassano, Berman, Gopinath, Narasimhan, Yao
title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
transfer: Memory of reflections works when the feedback is real (unit tests, environment). The base model and the AlfWorld 130/134 figure in the old brief were NOT confirmed here. Reported GPT-4 baseline of 80% is now outdated.

claim: Self-Refine (same model generates, critiques, revises) reported about 20% average absolute gain over one-step generation across 7 tasks with GPT-3.5, ChatGPT and GPT-4, by human and automatic metrics
authors: Madaan, Tandon, Gupta, Hallinan, Wiegreffe, Alon, Dziri, Prabhumoye, Yang, and others
title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
transfer: Missed by old brief. Contradicts Huang et al. on its face. Gains are mostly on open-ended generation scored by preference, not on reasoning with exact answers; weak first prompts inflate gains (Huang's point). Use only for style or open tasks, never single-answer reasoning.

claim: Process supervision significantly outperforms outcome supervision on MATH; the process-supervised reward model solved 78% of a representative MATH test subset; released PRM800K (800,000 step labels)
quote: process supervision significantly outperforms outcome supervision
authors: Lightman, Kosaraju, Burda, Edwards, Baker, Lee, Leike, Schulman, Sutskever, Cobbe
title: Let's Verify Step by Step
transfer: Needs a trained verifier; for us use program-run step checks. Confirms the 78% (the old brief's open item, now settled at 78% for the subset).

claim: Coverage (share of problems solved by any sample) grows log-linearly over four orders of magnitude of samples; SWE-bench Lite went from 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250 samples) with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct; without automatic verifiers, majority vote and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples
authors: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Re, Mirhoseini
title: Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
transfer: Sample wide only where a verifier exists. Selection, not generation, is the limit. Verifies old brief F4.

claim: Compute-optimal test-time scaling, allocating by prompt difficulty, gave over 4x better efficiency than best-of-N and in some cases beat a 14x larger model in a FLOPs-matched test
authors: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar
title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
n: MATH, PaLM-2 family (not stated in abstract)
transfer: Estimate difficulty first, then choose: easy ones revise or stop, hard ones search wider. Abstract says 'some problems', so the 14x claim is not general. Verifies old brief F6.

claim: Longer reasoning lowered accuracy on built tasks: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, deduction with constraint tracking; Claude models grow more distracted by irrelevant information, o-series overfit problem framing
quote: inverse scaling relationship between test-time compute and accuracy
authors: Gema, Hagele, Chen, Arditi, and 10 others including Perez
title: Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute
transfer: Cap reasoning length per task class and test across lengths; strip irrelevant context before reasoning. Verifies old brief F7.

claim: s1: fine-tuning Qwen2.5-32B on 1,000 reasoning traces plus budget forcing ('Wait' appended) raised AIME24 from 50% to 57% and beat o1-preview on competition math by up to 27%
authors: Muennighoff, Yang, Shi, Li, Fei-Fei, Hajishirzi, Zettlemoyer, Liang, Candes, Hashimoto
title: s1: Simple test-time scaling
transfer: Budget forcing was applied to a fine-tuned model; do not expect the same by prompting 'Wait'. Verifies old brief M6 caveat.

claim: Stated CoT is often unfaithful: biasing features (such as option order) shift answers while explanations omit them; accuracy fell as much as 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks with GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0
authors: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman
title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
transfer: New. A written rationale is not proof of the real reason. Do not use the model's own explanation as evidence of correctness; shuffle option order and compare answers as a bias probe.

claim: Intervening on CoT shows reliance varies by task; larger and more capable models give less faithful CoT on most tasks studied; CoT gain is not only extra compute or phrasing
quote: CoT can be faithful if the circumstances such as the model size and task are carefully chosen
authors: Lanham, Chen, Radhakrishnan, and others
title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
transfer: New. Truncate or corrupt a reasoning step and see if the answer changes: if not, that reasoning is decoration and can be cut to save tokens.

claim: Across over 350 LLMs, when two models both err they give the same wrong answer about 60% of the time on one leaderboard; shared architecture or provider raises correlation, and larger accurate models are highly correlated even across providers
quote: models agree 60% of the time when both models err
authors: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg
title: Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
transfer: New and directly on our finding that agreement is weak evidence. Samples from one model are even more correlated than across models, so vote count is not independent evidence; require an external check or a different-method path.

claim: Step-Back prompting (derive the principle first) with PaLM-2L improved MMLU Physics by 7%, MMLU Chemistry by 11%, TimeQA by 27%, MuSiQue by 7%; also tested on GPT-4 and Llama2-70B
authors: Zheng, Mishra, Chen, Cheng, Chi, Le, Zhou
title: Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models
transfer: One abstraction call before solving for knowledge-heavy science and multi-hop items. Same-lab authors as CoT/self-consistency/Self-Discover; no independent replication found in this pass.

claim: Self-Discover reported up to 32% gain over CoT on BigBench-Hard, grounded agent reasoning and MATH (GPT-4, PaLM 2), over 20 points above CoT-Self-Consistency with 10-40x less inference compute, with structures transferring across model families
quote: by as much as 32% compared to Chain of Thought (CoT)
authors: Zhou, Pujara, Ren, Chen, Cheng, Le, Chi, Zhou, Mishra, Zheng
title: Self-Discover: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
transfer: One planning call picks modules, then one solve call. Our own four-strategy schema lost on BrainTeaser, so gate by task class. 'Up to' is the best case. Claim of 'beat CoT-SC by 20 points' is as worded in the abstract summary.

claim: Analogical prompting (model writes its own relevant examples first) beat zero-shot CoT and manual few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench tasks; abstract gives no percentages
authors: Yasunaga, Chen, Li, Pasupat, Leskovec, Liang, Chi, Zhou
title: Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
transfer: The old brief's '+4% average' was NOT confirmed in the abstract; keep it unverified until the paper's table is read. Step: ask for 2 self-generated related solved problems before solving.

claim: Plan-and-Solve zero-shot prompting beat zero-shot CoT on all 10 datasets across 3 reasoning types with GPT-3, matched or beat zero-shot Program-of-Thought, and was comparable to 8-shot CoT on math; it targets missing-step errors, with calculation errors and misreading also identified as failure modes
authors: Wang, Xu, Lan, Hu, Lan, Lee, Lim
title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
transfer: Plan then execute in one call. Abstract has no percentages so the 'few points' in the old brief remains unverified. GPT-3 era; gains on modern models likely smaller (see 12-a-07).

claim: Models with 3B parameters or fewer do not consistently benefit from long CoT or from distillation of a strong reasoner, and do better fine-tuned on shorter simpler chains (Small Model Learnability Gap)
authors: Li, Yue, Xu, Jiang, Niu, Lin, Ramasubramanian, Poovendran
title: Small Models Struggle to Learn from Strong Reasoners
transfer: About fine-tuning, not prompting. For a small model prefer short chains and programmatic checks over long self-generated reasoning. Verifies old brief F3.
